title: David’s sons and Ira: “chief rulers”, or priests?
summary: The KJV calls David’s sons “chief rulers” and Ira “a chief ruler about David”. The Hebrew word in both places is the word the KJV translates “the priests” in the verse just before each. The Greek has “priest” for Ira.
text: KJV 2 Samuel 8:17: “Zadok the son of Ahitub, and Ahimelech the son of Abiathar, were the priests”. KJV 8:18: “and David's sons were chief rulers”. Hebrew (WLC) 8:17: כֹּהֲנִ֑ים [priests]; 8:18: וּבְנֵ֥י דָוִ֖ד כֹּהֲנִ֥ים הָיֽוּ [and the sons of David were priests]. Aleppo-based edition (HAC) 8:18: ובני דוד כהנים היו. KJV 20:25: “Zadok and Abiathar were the priests”. KJV 20:26: “And Ira also the Jairite was a chief ruler about David.” Hebrew (WLC) 20:25: כֹּהֲנִֽים; 20:26: הָיָ֥ה כֹהֵ֖ן לְדָוִֽד [was a priest to David]. HAC 20:26: היה כהן לדוד. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 8:18: καὶ οἱ υἱοὶ Δαυὶδ αὐλάρχαι ἦσαν [and the sons of David were chiefs of the court]; 20:25: ἱερεῖς [priests]; 20:26: ἦν ἱερεὺς τῷ Δαυίδ [was priest to David]. KJV 1 Chronicles 18:17: “and the sons of David were chief about the king”. Hebrew (WLC) 1 Chronicles 18:17: וּבְנֵי־דָוִ֥יד הָרִאשֹׁנִ֖ים לְיַ֥ד הַמֶּֽלֶךְ [and the sons of David were the first at the king’s side]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/10/8/, https://bolls.life/get-text/HAC/10/8/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/10/20/, https://bolls.life/get-text/HAC/10/20/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2SA08.htm, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2SA20.htm and https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/13/18/.
reasoning: In each list the same Hebrew noun appears in two adjoining verses. The KJV translates it “the priests” for Zadok and his colleague and “chief rulers” or “a chief ruler” for David’s sons and Ira. A priest and a chief ruler are different offices, so the KJV wording differs in meaning from the Hebrew at 8:18 and 20:26. The parallel verse in Chronicles is worded differently in Hebrew and does not use the noun.
scope: H rests on 8:18 and 20:26. G rests on 20:26 only, where Brenton’s Greek agrees with the Hebrew against the KJV. At 8:18 Brenton’s Greek has a court title, not “priests”, so 8:18 is not a G finding. No claim is made about what duties David’s sons or Ira performed, or about how their office relates to the priesthood of Aaron’s line. title: The Philistine images: burned, or carried off?
summary: The KJV of 2 Samuel says David and his men “burned” the abandoned images. The Hebrew and the Greek of that verse say they took them. Burning is what the parallel in 1 Chronicles says, with a different Hebrew verb.
text: KJV 2 Samuel 5:21: “And there they left their images, and David and his men burned them.” Hebrew (WLC): וַיִּשָּׂאֵ֥ם דָּוִ֖ד וַאֲנָשָֽׁיו [and David and his men lifted them, that is, carried them off]. Aleppo-based edition (HAC): וישאם דוד ואנשיו. The same verb earlier in the book: 2:32 וַיִּשְׂאוּ֙ אֶת־עֲשָׂהאֵ֔ל, KJV “And they took up Asahel”; 4:4 וַתִּשָּׂאֵ֤הוּ אֹֽמַנְתֹּו֙, KJV “his nurse took him up”. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 5:21: καὶ ἐλάβοσαν αὐτοὺς Δαυὶδ καὶ οἱ ἄνδρες [and David and the men took them]. KJV 1 Chronicles 14:12: “David gave a commandment, and they were burned with fire”. Hebrew (WLC) 1 Chronicles 14:12: וַיִּשָּׂרְפ֖וּ בָּאֵֽשׁ [and they were burned with fire]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/10/5/, https://bolls.life/get-text/HAC/10/5/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/10/2/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/10/4/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2SA05.htm and https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/13/14/.
reasoning: The Hebrew verb in 2 Samuel 5:21 is the verb for lifting and carrying, which the KJV translates “took up” at 2:32 and 4:4. Burning is a different act, and the Hebrew of Chronicles states it with a different verb and the words “with fire”. The KJV of Samuel therefore says what the Hebrew of Chronicles says, not what the Hebrew of Samuel says. With the Hebrew wording, Samuel has David’s men carry the images off and Chronicles has them burned at David’s order.
scope: Carrying the images off and then burning them could both have happened; neither book says both, and this record does not call the two Hebrew statements incompatible. The finding is the difference between the KJV and the Hebrew and Greek of 2 Samuel 5:21. The Greek agrees with the Hebrew against the KJV, so both H and G apply. title: Hadadezer’s horsemen: 1,700, 700 or 7,000?
summary: The Hebrew of 2 Samuel 8:4 says David took “a thousand and seven hundred horsemen”. The KJV makes that a thousand chariots and seven hundred horsemen. Chronicles and the Greek of Samuel have a thousand chariots and seven thousand horsemen.
text: KJV 2 Samuel 8:4: “And David took from him a thousand chariots, and seven hundred horsemen, and twenty thousand footmen”. Hebrew (WLC): אֶ֤לֶף וּשְׁבַע־מֵאֹות֙ פָּרָשִׁ֔ים וְעֶשְׂרִ֥ים אֶ֖לֶף אִ֣ישׁ רַגְלִ֑י [a thousand and seven hundred horsemen and twenty thousand footmen]. Aleppo-based edition (HAC): אלף ושבע מאות פרשים ועשרים אלף איש רגלי. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 8:4: χίλια ἅρματα, καὶ ἑπτὰ χιλιάδας ἱππέων, καὶ εἴκοσι χιλιάδας ἀνδρῶν πεζῶν [a thousand chariots, and seven thousand horsemen, and twenty thousand footmen]. KJV 1 Chronicles 18:4: “And David took from him a thousand chariots, and seven thousand horsemen, and twenty thousand footmen”. Hebrew (WLC) 1 Chronicles 18:4: אֶ֣לֶף רֶ֗כֶב וְשִׁבְעַ֤ת אֲלָפִים֙ פָּֽרָשִׁ֔ים [a thousand chariots and seven thousand horsemen]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/10/8/, https://bolls.life/get-text/HAC/10/8/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2SA08.htm and https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/13/18/.
reasoning: In the Hebrew of Samuel there is no word for chariots between “a thousand” and “seven hundred”; the two numbers join into one figure for horsemen. The KJV divides them into two groups, which changes the count of horsemen from 1,700 to 700 and adds a count of chariots. Chronicles, in Hebrew and in the KJV, has a thousand chariots and seven thousand horsemen, and so does Brenton’s Greek of Samuel. The footmen are twenty thousand in all of them.
scope: H: the KJV count of horsemen differs from the Hebrew count. G: the Greek count of horsemen (seven thousand) differs from the KJV count (seven hundred); here the Greek does not agree with the Hebrew either. The end of the Hebrew verse does mention chariots, so the record does not say none were taken; it says the Hebrew gives no number for them. No claim is made about which figure is original. title: Eighteen thousand in the valley of salt: Syrians, or Edomites?
summary: In 2 Samuel David strikes eighteen thousand Syrians in the valley of salt. In 1 Chronicles Abishai strikes eighteen thousand Edomites there. The Greek of 2 Samuel has Idumea, not Syria.
text: KJV 2 Samuel 8:13: “And David gat him a name when he returned from smiting of the Syrians in the valley of salt, being eighteen thousand men.” Hebrew (WLC): מֵהַכֹּותֹ֥ו אֶת־אֲרָ֖ם בְּגֵיא־מֶ֑לַח שְׁמֹונָ֥ה עָשָׂ֖ר אָֽלֶף [from his striking Aram in the valley of salt, eighteen thousand]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 8:13: ἐπάταξε τὴν Ἰδουμαίαν ἐν Γεβελὲμ εἰς ὀκτωκαίδεκα χιλιάδας [he struck Idumea in Gebelem, to eighteen thousand]. KJV 1 Chronicles 18:12: “Moreover Abishai the son of Zeruiah slew of the Edomites in the valley of salt eighteen thousand.” Hebrew (WLC) 1 Chronicles 18:12: הִכָּ֤ה אֶת־אֱדֹום֙ בְּגֵ֣יא הַמֶּ֔לַח שְׁמֹונָ֥ה עָשָׂ֖ר אָֽלֶף [struck Edom in the valley of salt, eighteen thousand]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/10/8/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2SA08.htm and https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/13/18/.
reasoning: The place and the number are the same in both books. The people struck are Syrians (Hebrew Aram) in Samuel and Edomites (Hebrew Edom) in Chronicles. Brenton’s Greek of Samuel names Idumea, so it differs from the KJV of Samuel on who was struck.

title: How Ishbosheth’s killers got in: fetching wheat, or a sleeping doorkeeper?
summary: In the KJV the two brothers enter “as though they would have fetched wheat” and strike Ishbosheth. In the Greek of that verse a doorkeeper who was cleaning wheat falls asleep and the brothers slip past; no blow is struck until the next verse.
text: KJV 2 Samuel 4:6: “And they came thither into the midst of the house, as though they would have fetched wheat; and they smote him under the fifth rib: and Rechab and Baanah his brother escaped.” KJV 4:7: “and they smote him, and slew him, and beheaded him”. Hebrew (WLC) 4:6: לֹקְחֵ֣י חִטִּ֔ים וַיַּכֻּ֖הוּ אֶל־הַחֹ֑מֶשׁ [fetchers of wheat, and they struck him in the belly]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 4:6: Καὶ ἰδοὺ ἡ θυρωρὸς τοῦ οἴκου ἐκάθαιρε πυροὺς, καὶ ἐνύσταξε καὶ ἐκάθευδε· καὶ Ῥηχὰβ καὶ Βαανὰ οἱ ἀδελφοὶ διέλαθον [And behold, the doorkeeper of the house was cleaning wheat, and she nodded and slept; and Rechab and Baana the brothers slipped by]. Brenton Greek 4:7: καὶ τύπτουσιν αὐτὸν, καὶ θανατοῦσιν αὐτὸν [and they strike him and put him to death]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/10/4/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2SA04.htm.
reasoning: The KJV of verse 6 has the brothers come in under a pretence, strike, and escape, and verse 7 then tells the killing again. The Greek of verse 6 has no pretence and no blow. It has a doorkeeper, a person the KJV does not mention anywhere in the chapter, and the wheat belongs to her work, not to the brothers’ excuse. The killing itself comes once, in verse 7.
scope: The two accounts of the entry are different, but they are not shown to be incompatible: a doorkeeper could sleep and the brothers could still carry a pretext. The killing in verse 7 is the same in both. No H tag: the KJV follows the Hebrew of verse 6. No claim is made about which form of the verse is older. summary: Amasa’s father is “Ithra an Israelite” in 2 Samuel and “Jether the Ishmeelite” in 1 Chronicles. The Greek of 2 Samuel calls him a Jezraelite.

Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 17:25: Ἰεθὲρ ὁ Ἰεζραηλίτης [Jether the Jezraelite]. KJV 1 Chronicles 2:17: “and the father of Amasa was Jether the Ishmeelite”. Hebrew (WLC) 1 Chronicles 2:17: יֶ֖תֶר הַיִּשְׁמְעֵאלִֽי [Jether the Ishmaelite]. Brenton Greek 1 Chronicles 2:17: ὁ Ἰσμαηλίτης. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/10/17/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2SA17.htm, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/13/2/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/1CH02.htm.
reasoning: Both verses name the father of the same Amasa, son of Abigail. The KJV and the Hebrew call him an Israelite in one book and an Ishmeelite in the other, which are different peoples. Brenton’s Greek of Samuel has a third word and so differs from the KJV there; in Chronicles the Greek agrees with the KJV.
scope: A man might be called by where he lived as well as by descent; neither verse says that of Amasa’s father. The record compares the words printed and does not decide which is original. title: Seven or three years of famine?
summary: Gad offers David seven years of famine in 2 Samuel and three in 1 Chronicles. The Hebrew has the same two numbers. The Greek of 2 Samuel has three, as Chronicles does.
text: KJV 2 Samuel 24:13: “Shall seven years of famine come unto thee in thy land?” Hebrew (WLC): שֶֽׁבַע שָׁנִ֣ים ׀ רָעָ֣ב [seven years of famine]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 2 Samuel 24:13: εἰ ἔλθῃ σοι τρία ἔτη λιμὸς ἐν τῇ γῇ σου [whether three years of famine shall come to you in your land]. Brenton Greek 1 Chronicles 21:12: ἢ τρία ἔτη λιμοῦ [either three years of famine]. summary: 2 Samuel 14:27 says three sons were born to Absalom. 2 Samuel 18:18 has Absalom set up a pillar because, he says, “I have no son to keep my name in remembrance”.
text: KJV 2 Samuel 14:27: “And unto Absalom there were born three sons, and one daughter, whose name was Tamar”.
